name: El
symbol: seated bearded elder on a throne, sometimes with bull horns on his crown

cultCenter.name: Ugarit (Ras Shamra), Syrian coast; his mythic tent stood 'at the source of the two rivers'

family.name: the 'seventy sons of Athirat', the gods of the council

family.relation: household member (called 'son of Dagan' in the texts)
family.name: Baal-Hadad

plain:
El is simply the old West Semitic word for 'god', and also the name of the high god who ruled over all the other gods in Canaanite religion. At Ugarit he is a wise, grey-bearded father figure who sits enthroned and hands down decisions to a council of younger gods.

The Bible uses the same word constantly for Israel's God (El Shaddai, El Elyon, Bethel = 'house of El', Israel = perhaps 'El strives'). Unlike Baal, El is almost never attacked in the Bible. That is because Israel's writers treated El either as an ordinary word for God or as another name of the one God they worshipped. How much of Canaanite El was absorbed into Israel's picture of Yahweh is a real and open question among scholars.
myth:
In the clay tablets from Ugarit (14th to 13th century BC), El is 'Father of Years', 'Bull El', 'Creator of Creatures' and 'Kind El, the Compassionate'. He lives in a tent-shrine on a mountain at the springs of the two rivers and the two deeps. The gods are his children and meet in 'the assembly of El'.

El does not fight. He decides. When Yam (Sea) wants supremacy, El grants it; when Baal needs a palace, Baal and Anat must win El's permission, usually by going through his wife Athirat. Anat even threatens the old god to get her way. When Baal dies, El comes down from his throne, sits in the dust, gashes his skin and mourns. Then he dreams that the heavens rain oil and the wadis run with honey, and knows that Baal lives again. One text (the 'Birth of the Gracious Gods') describes El fathering gods in a frank, earthy scene by the sea.
biblicalRole:
El is the one Canaanite god the Bible does not fight. The patriarchs meet God under El names: El Elyon ('God Most High', Gen 14:18-22), El Roi (Gen 16:13), El Shaddai (Gen 17:1), El Olam (Gen 21:33), El-Elohe-Israel (Gen 33:20). Exod 6:3 says God appeared to the patriarchs as El Shaddai but was not known to them by the name Yahweh.

Some biblical poetry describes God with language that matches El at Ugarit: an aged figure on a throne with white hair (Dan 7:9), the 'divine assembly' (Ps 82:1, adat-el), and the Most High dividing the nations (Deut 32:8). Melchizedek's title for God, 'Most High, creator (or possessor) of heaven and earth' (Gen 14:19), matches a Phoenician title of El found at Karatepe.

How to read this is debated. (1) Many critical scholars (Frank Moore Cross, Mark S. Smith) argue that Yahweh and El were originally separate gods and that Israel merged them, so that Yahweh took over El's role as head of the council. (2) Others argue Israel always used 'El' as a generic word and title for its own God, so the overlap is about shared language, not borrowed gods. (3) Traditional Jewish and Christian readers see the patriarchs worshipping the one true God under the common word for God, with the name Yahweh revealed more fully at the exodus.

encounters.title: Melchizedek blesses Abram by El Elyon
encounters.summary: The priest-king of Salem blesses Abram by 'God Most High, creator of heaven and earth', and Abram identifies this God with Yahweh in his oath.

encounters.title: Jacob names Bethel and builds an altar to El
encounters.summary: Jacob names places after El: Bethel ('house of El') and El-Elohe-Israel ('El, the God of Israel').

encounters.title: God reveals the name Yahweh
encounters.summary: God tells Moses that he appeared to the patriarchs as El Shaddai, but by the name Yahweh he did not make himself known to them.

encounters.title: The Most High divides the nations
encounters.summary: Elyon apportions the nations, and Yahweh's portion is Jacob. Whether Elyon and Yahweh are the same figure here is debated; most traditional readers say yes.

encounters.title: God stands in the divine assembly
encounters.summary: God takes his stand in the 'assembly of El' and judges the gods. The phrase matches Ugaritic language for El's council.

encounters.title: The Ancient of Days
encounters.summary: Daniel sees an aged figure with white hair enthroned among a court, a picture many scholars compare to El, the Father of Years.

archaeology.summary: Hundreds of alphabetic cuneiform tablets, written c. 1400-1185 BC, describe El as father of the gods, head of their assembly, aged and wise. They are the main source for Canaanite El.

A limestone stele shows a seated, bearded god with a horned crown receiving homage from a king, and a gold-plated bronze figure shows a seated elder god. Both are often identified as El, but neither is labelled.
An 8th-century BC Phoenician text invokes 'El, creator of earth', a title close to Melchizedek's 'God Most High, creator of heaven and earth' in Gen 14:19.

A c. 800 BC text about 'Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods' mentions El and a group of gods called shaddayin. It shows the same El vocabulary on the east side of the Jordan and a Balaam tradition outside the Bible.

laterFate: El never became a demon. The word simply lived on: in Hebrew as a term for God, in names like Israel, Samuel, Michael, Gabriel and Immanuel, and in the related Aramaic elah and Arabic ilah (from which Allah derives). In Phoenician religion of the first millennium El faded behind city gods like Melqart and Baal Shamem; Philo of Byblos (via Eusebius) equated him with the Greek Kronos.

name: Asherah
symbol: stylised tree or wooden pole; nude goddess between lions or ibexes

cultCenter.name: Samaria, where Ahab set up an asherah (worshipped at Ugarit as Athirat and in Judah's high places)

family.name: the seventy sons of Athirat (the gods)

family.relation: consort (claimed in some Israelite inscriptions; debated)
family.name: Yahweh

plain:
Asherah was the great mother-goddess of Canaan, wife of the high god El. In the Bible the word 'asherah' means two connected things: the goddess herself, and a wooden pole or stylised tree set up beside altars to stand for her. That is why the Bible talks about asherahs being 'made', 'planted', 'cut down' and 'burned'.

What makes Asherah famous today is a set of Hebrew inscriptions from about 800-700 BC that bless people 'by Yahweh and his asherah'. They show that at least some Israelites put Asherah, or her symbol, right next to Israel's God. The prophets and the reforming kings fought this for centuries.
myth: At Ugarit she is Athirat, 'Lady Athirat of the Sea' (the exact meaning of the title is debated, perhaps 'she who treads on the sea'), wife of El and 'creatress of the gods', mother of seventy divine sons. She nurses royal heirs in the Kirta epic. In the Baal Cycle she first sides with Yam against Baal, but when Baal and Anat bring her gifts she rides on a donkey to El's tent and persuades him to let Baal build his palace. After Baal dies, she proposes one of her sons, Athtar, as replacement king; he is too small to fill Baal's throne. So she is the queen mother of heaven: the one who has El's ear.
biblicalRole:
Asherah appears about 40 times in the Bible. Most uses are the wooden cult object: Israel is told not to plant any tree as an asherah beside Yahweh's altar (Deut 16:21) and to cut down the Canaanites' asherim (Exod 34:13; Deut 7:5). Gideon cuts down his father's asherah beside the altar of Baal (Judg 6:25-28).

Some passages clearly mean the goddess: 400 'prophets of Asherah' eat at Jezebel's table (1 Kgs 18:19); Josiah removes vessels made 'for Baal and for Asherah' (2 Kgs 23:4). Queen mother Maacah made an 'abominable image for Asherah' and was deposed for it (1 Kgs 15:13). Manasseh put a carved image of Asherah inside Yahweh's temple (2 Kgs 21:7). Josiah took it out, burned it at the Kidron, ground it to dust and threw the dust on the common graves; he also tore down the rooms in the temple where women wove hangings for Asherah (2 Kgs 23:6-7).

The repeated fight suggests Asherah worship was not a foreign import but a deep-rooted part of popular religion in both Israel and Judah. The biblical writers present it as apostasy; many historians see it as the older popular religion that the prophets and reforming kings set out to remove. Both statements can be true at once.

encounters.title: Do not plant an asherah beside Yahweh's altar
encounters.summary: The law forbids setting up an asherah or standing stone next to Yahweh's altar, which implies people were doing exactly that.

encounters.title: Gideon cuts down his father's asherah
encounters.summary: Gideon tears down his father's Baal altar and the asherah beside it, then uses its wood to burn a sacrifice to Yahweh.

encounters.title: Queen mother Maacah deposed
encounters.summary: King Asa removes his grandmother from her position because she made an image for Asherah, and burns it at the Kidron.

encounters.title: Jezebel's 400 prophets of Asherah
encounters.summary: Ahab makes an asherah in Samaria; Jezebel feeds 450 prophets of Baal and 400 of Asherah. Only Baal's prophets appear at the Carmel contest itself.

encounters.title: Manasseh puts Asherah in the temple
encounters.summary: Manasseh sets up a carved image of Asherah in the house where Yahweh had said he would put his name.

encounters.title: Josiah burns Asherah
encounters.summary: Josiah removes the Asherah from the temple, burns and grinds it, scatters its dust on graves, and pulls down the women's weaving rooms. He also cuts down asherim at Bethel and elsewhere.

encounters.title: Prophets condemn the asherim
encounters.summary: Prophets list the asherim beside altars on hills and under green trees as part of what brought judgement.

archaeology.summary: Storage jars at a c. 800 BC caravan way-station carry blessings 'by Yahweh of Samaria and his asherah' and 'by Yahweh of Teman and his asherah'. Drawings on the same jar show two Bes-like figures and a seated lyre player; whether any of them depict Yahweh and Asherah is disputed, and most specialists think the standing pair are Bes figures.

A late 8th-century BC tomb inscription for one Uriyahu says he is blessed by Yahweh and that 'by his asherah' Yahweh saved him from his enemies. The text is damaged and its reading is partly uncertain.

Biblical Hebrew normally does not put a possessive ending ('his') on a personal name, so many read 'his asherah' as Yahweh's cult object, the pole or tree. Others argue the object and the goddess were never really separable, or that the grammar rule has exceptions, so the texts show a belief that Yahweh had a consort. A third view reads it as a place or shrine. The question is unresolved.

archaeology.find: Tel Arad shrine and its two altars (residue study 2020)
archaeology.summary: A small shrine inside a Judahite royal fortress had standing stones and two limestone incense altars at the entrance to its niche. A 2020 study (Arie, Rosen and Namdar, *Tel Aviv*) found frankincense mixed with animal fat on one altar and cannabis mixed with animal dung on the other: the earliest known evidence of a mind-altering substance in Judah's worship. The shrine, dated to the 8th century BC, was deliberately buried; the excavators tied this to Hezekiah's reform, others to Josiah or to other causes. Whether the two stones or altars stood for Yahweh and a consort such as Asherah is an attractive guess, not a finding.

A 10th-century BC clay stand has four tiers: one shows a nude female between two lions, another a sacred tree flanked by ibexes and lions. Many read these as Asherah and her tree symbol (Ruth Hestrin's interpretation); the top tier shows an animal under a winged sun.

archaeology.place: Jerusalem, Lachish and many Judahite sites
archaeology.summary: Hundreds of small clay women holding their breasts, common c. 750-586 BC in Judean homes. Many scholars (e.g. William Dever) link them to Asherah; others see them as generic fertility charms or images of worshippers.

laterFate: Asherah disappeared from Jewish worship after the exile, but the word survived in strange ways. The Greek Septuagint and Latin Vulgate often translated asherah as 'grove' (alsos, lucus), so the King James Version speaks of 'groves', and generations of readers did not know a goddess lay behind the word. The Mishnah (tractate Avodah Zarah) still discusses what makes a tree an asherah. Asherah has no prominent place in Milton's catalogue or in medieval demon lists. Since the Kuntillet Ajrud discoveries she has become a popular subject in books and documentaries about 'God's wife', a framing that the evidence supports only in part.

name: Baal (Hadad)
otherNames: Baal Shamem ('lord of heaven', later Phoenician)
Melqart (Baal of Tyre, a related city god)
original: Hebrew ba'al ('lord, owner, husband'); Ugaritic b'l, hd
symbol: bull; warrior with raised club and a spear sprouting into lightning

cultCenter.name: Mount Zaphon (Jebel Aqra), 1,717 m, on the Syrian-Turkish border; temple of Baal on the acropolis of Ugarit

family.relation: head of the household he belongs to
family.name: El

plain:
'Baal' is not really a name. It is a title meaning 'lord', 'owner' or 'husband'. The god most often meant by it is Hadad, the storm god who brings thunder and, above all, rain.

That matters because of geography. Egypt was watered by the Nile and Mesopotamia by the Tigris and Euphrates. Canaan lived or died by rainfall, as Deuteronomy itself points out (Deut 11:10-11). A god who controlled the rain controlled the harvest, so for farmers Baal was the obvious god to keep happy. The Bible's long struggle against Baal, from Judges to Jeremiah, is a struggle over who really sends the rain.
myth:
The Baal Cycle, six tablets from Ugarit written down by the scribe Ilimilku around the 14th or 13th century BC, tells Baal's story in three episodes.

1. Baal and Yam. Yam (Sea) is made king by El and demands that Baal be handed over. The craftsman god Kothar-wa-Khasis makes Baal two magic clubs, 'Driver' and 'Chaser'. The second strikes Yam down. Baal is acclaimed king.

2. Baal's palace. A king needs a house. With Anat's help and Athirat's persuasion, El allows it, and Kothar builds a palace of gold, silver and lapis on Mount Zaphon. Kothar proposes a window; Baal at first refuses, then agrees, and through it he thunders his voice across the earth. (Why he hesitated is debated; one guess links it to the line 'death has come up into our windows', Jer 9:21.)

3. Baal and Mot. Mot (Death) invites Baal to his realm. Baal goes down into Death's throat and dies; the land dries out. El and Anat mourn; Anat buries him on Zaphon. Anat then seizes Mot, splits him with a blade, winnows, burns, grinds and sows him like grain. El dreams of heavens raining oil, and Baal returns. Seven years later Baal and Mot fight again until the sun goddess Shapash separates them.

Many scholars read this as a seasonal myth of the dry summer and the return of the autumn rains. Others (e.g. Mark S. Smith) caution that it is mainly about kingship and the fragile order of the world, not a neat annual calendar.
biblicalRole:
Baal is Yahweh's chief rival in the historical books. Israel 'yoked itself' to Baal-peor in the wilderness (Num 25:3). In Judges, each slide into apostasy is described as serving 'the Baals' (Judg 2:11-13). Gideon tears down his father's Baal altar and is nicknamed Jerubbaal, 'let Baal contend' (Judg 6:25-32).

The big confrontation comes under Ahab, who married Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and built a Baal temple in Samaria (1 Kgs 16:31-32). Which Baal Jezebel promoted is debated: Melqart of Tyre, Baal Shamem, or Hadad. Elijah announces a drought: no dew or rain except at his word (1 Kgs 17:1), a direct challenge to the rain god. On Mount Carmel the contest is fought on Baal's home ground: fire from the sky, then rain (1 Kgs 18). Jehu later massacres Baal's worshippers and turns his Samaria temple into a latrine (2 Kgs 10:18-28); in Judah Athaliah's Baal temple falls with her (2 Kgs 11:18).

The prophets keep fighting. Hosea says Israel did not know it was Yahweh who gave the grain, wine and oil she credited to Baal, and that one day she will no longer call God 'my Baal' (Hos 2:8; Hos 2:16-17). Jeremiah, some three centuries after Elijah, still condemns Baal altars and child burning 'to Baal' (Jer 2:23; Jer 19:5).

The Bible also borrows Baal's imagery for Yahweh: the one who 'rides on the clouds' (Ps 68:4; Ps 104:3; Isa 19:1), whose thunderous voice shakes the cedars (Ps 29), and who crushes the sea monster. Many scholars think Ps 29 adapts a Canaanite storm hymn; others see shared regional poetry rather than borrowing. The point in either case is polemical: the titles Baal claimed belong to Yahweh.

encounters.title: The cycle of Judges: 'they served the Baals'
encounters.summary: Each generation abandons Yahweh for the Baals and Ashtaroth and falls to its enemies.

encounters.title: Gideon becomes Jerubbaal
encounters.summary: Gideon pulls down his father's altar to Baal. His father says, if Baal is a god, let him contend for himself; Gideon gets the name Jerubbaal.

encounters.title: Ahab, Jezebel and the Baal temple in Samaria
encounters.summary: Ahab marries the Sidonian princess Jezebel, builds a house of Baal in Samaria and makes an asherah.

encounters.title: Drought announced
encounters.summary: Elijah declares no dew or rain except at his word, striking at the storm god's own domain.

encounters.title: The contest on Mount Carmel
encounters.summary: Baal's 450 prophets call on him from morning to noon. Elijah mocks: perhaps he is musing, or has 'turned aside' (possibly a euphemism for relieving himself; debated), or is travelling, or asleep. They gash themselves, a mourning rite; El himself gashes his skin over the dead Baal at Ugarit. Elijah soaks his altar with twelve jars of water; fire falls and consumes it. The people cry, 'Yahweh, he is God.'

encounters.title: Rain returns
encounters.summary: After the contest a small cloud rises from the sea and heavy rain falls: Yahweh, not Baal, ends the drought.

encounters.title: Jehu destroys the Baal temple
encounters.summary: Jehu gathers Baal's worshippers into his temple in Samaria, kills them, breaks the pillar and makes the building a latrine.

encounters.title: Seven thousand who did not bow
encounters.summary: God tells Elijah he has kept 7,000 who have not knelt to Baal; Paul applies this to a faithful remnant.

encounters.title: Hosea: 'You will no longer call me my Baal'
encounters.summary: Israel credited Baal with the grain, wine and oil that Yahweh gave. Hosea plays on ba'al as 'husband': Israel will call God 'my husband' (ishi) instead.

encounters.title: Jeremiah's long fight
encounters.summary: Jeremiah condemns altars to 'the shameful thing' (bosheth), to Baal, and the burning of children 'to Baal' in the Hinnom valley.

archaeology.find: Ugarit and the Baal Cycle tablets
archaeology.year: 1928 discovery; excavations from 1929 under Claude Schaeffer
archaeology.place: Ras Shamra and Minet el-Beida, Syria
archaeology.summary: A farmer's plough opened a tomb at Minet el-Beida in 1928; digs at Ras Shamra began in 1929 and the first tablets appeared that May. The new alphabetic cuneiform was deciphered in 1930 by Hans Bauer, Edouard Dhorme and Charles Virolleaud. The Baal Cycle (KTU 1.1-1.6) is the fullest account of Baal's myths.

archaeology.place: Near the temple of Baal, Ugarit (now in the Louvre)
archaeology.summary: A limestone stele shows the storm god striding with a raised club and holding a spear whose shaft sprouts like a plant or lightning. It is the classic image of Baal.
8th-century BC administrative notes from the royal palace include personal names compounded with Baal alongside many with Yahweh, showing both were in use in the northern kingdom.
A fragmentary wall text in Phoenician script mentions Baal and El in a theophany-like setting (mountains melting), alongside the Yahweh texts found there.

renamed.original: Eshbaal ('man of Baal'), Merib-baal ('Baal is advocate'), Jerubbaal ('let Baal contend')
renamed.explanation: Chronicles keeps the original names of Saul's son and grandson, Eshbaal and Merib-baal (1 Chr 8:33-34). Samuel calls them Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth (2 Sam 2:8; 2 Sam 4:4), and calls Gideon Jerubbesheth (2 Sam 11:21). Bosheth means 'shame'. The standard explanation is that scribes replaced 'Baal' with 'shame' to avoid saying the god's name; Jeremiah and Hosea themselves call Baal 'the shame' (Jer 11:13; Hos 9:10). In Saul's time 'baal' could still be used innocently of Yahweh as 'lord'. A minority view argues that bosheth was once an honourable divine epithet (compare Akkadian bashtu, 'dignity'), so not every change is an insult.

laterFate: Hadad survived for centuries in Syria: as Hadad of Damascus (Rimmon), as Zeus Kasios on his old mountain Zaphon (where the Roman emperors Hadrian and Julian are reported to have climbed to sacrifice), and as Jupiter Heliopolitanus at Baalbek in Lebanon, whose name preserves 'Baal'. In Christian thought the Baals became demons. Milton's *Paradise Lost* (Book 1) lists 'Baalim and Ashtaroth' together among the fallen angels, and early modern demon lists include a 'Bael' or 'Baal' as a king of hell. 'Baal' is still used in English as a byword for a false god.

name: Anat
otherNames: Sister-in-law of the peoples (title, meaning debated)
symbol: young warrior goddess with axe, shield and spear, sometimes winged

cultCenter.name: Ugarit (also worshipped in Egypt and at Elephantine)

family.relation: brother and ally (possibly also lover; debated)
family.name: Baal-Hadad

plain:
Anat was Canaan's fiercest goddess: a young warrior who fights for her brother Baal. In one famous scene she slaughters an army and wades knee-deep, then neck-deep, in blood, with severed heads hung at her waist. When Baal dies she hunts down Death himself and destroys him.

The Bible never names her as a goddess, but her name survives in place names and personal names (Anathoth, Jeremiah's home town; Shamgar 'son of Anath'), which shows she was once known in the land.
myth:
In the Baal Cycle Anat battles armies 'from the seashore to the sunrise', wading through blood, then hosts a feast. She threatens El with violence to get Baal his palace. When Baal dies she searches the earth for him, weeps until she is full of tears, carries his body to Zaphon and buries him. Then she seizes Mot and destroys him as a farmer treats grain: she splits him with a blade, winnows him, burns him, grinds him and sows him in the field, and the birds eat his flesh. In the Aqhat epic she covets a magic bow belonging to the young hero Aqhat, offers him immortality for it, is rebuffed, and has him killed, after which the land suffers drought.

She is called 'virgin' or 'maiden', yet some texts seem to describe a sexual union with Baal; whether these are about Anat and what 'virgin' means here are debated.
biblicalRole: Anat is not named as a deity in the Hebrew Bible. Her name survives in: Anathoth, a Levitical town and Jeremiah's birthplace (Josh 21:18; Jer 1:1); Beth-anath ('house of Anat') in Naphtali, which the Israelites did not conquer (Josh 19:38; Judg 1:33); and the judge Shamgar 'son of Anath' (Judg 3:31; Judg 5:6), possibly a warrior title ('son of Anat' = a soldier under her protection) rather than his parent's name. Some scholars suggest she is among the candidates for the 'Queen of Heaven' of Jeremiah, since Egyptian texts call her 'lady of heaven'; this is one option among several.

encounters.title: Shamgar son of Anath
encounters.summary: A judge who killed 600 Philistines with an ox-goad bears Anat's name, perhaps as a family name or a warrior title.

encounters.title: Beth-anath left unconquered
encounters.summary: A town named 'house of Anat' stood in Naphtali's territory; its Canaanite inhabitants remained.

encounters.title: Anathoth, Jeremiah's home town
encounters.summary: The priestly town of Anathoth near Jerusalem probably carries a plural form of Anat's name, an echo of earlier worship there.

archaeology.find: Ugaritic Baal Cycle and Aqhat epic
archaeology.summary: The main sources for Anat's character as a violent, loyal warrior goddess.
Anat was adopted into Egyptian religion as a war goddess; Ramesses II named a daughter Bint-Anat ('daughter of Anat') and called Anat his protector in battle.

Aramaic documents from a 5th-century BC Jewish military colony list contributions for Yaho (Yahweh) and also mention Anat-Yahu and Anat-Bethel. Whether Anat-Yahu was a consort of Yahweh, an aspect of him, or a separate goddess is debated.

laterFate: Anat faded in the first millennium BC. In Cyprus a bilingual inscription equates her with Athena. Many scholars think she contributed, with Astarte, to the later Syrian goddess Atargatis, though the etymology is debated. She has little place in Christian demonology and is absent from Milton's catalogue.

name: Astarte
symbol: nude goddess, sometimes on a horse or lion; star or crescent; the 'womb of the flock'

cultCenter.name: Sidon (also Tyre, Kition in Cyprus, Carthage, Egypt)

plain:
Astarte (Hebrew Ashtoreth) was the Phoenician goddess of love, war and fertility, the western cousin of Mesopotamia's Ishtar. She was the city goddess of Sidon, and the Phoenicians carried her across the Mediterranean to Cyprus, Carthage and beyond.

In the Bible she appears as 'Ashtoreth of the Sidonians', for whom Solomon built a shrine, and in the plural 'Ashtaroth', paired with 'the Baals' as shorthand for all the foreign gods Israel kept turning to.
myth: Astarte has no long surviving myth of her own at Ugarit, where she appears mostly as a hunter and warrior who rebukes Baal for gloating over Yam ('scatter him!'), and as the 'name of Baal'. In Egypt she became a war goddess riding a horse with weapons. In Phoenicia she was a royal goddess: the kings of Sidon served as her priests. Greek writers identified her with Aphrodite; Herodotus calls the temple of Aphrodite Ourania at the Philistine city of Ashkelon the oldest of its kind. Lucian's *On the Syrian Goddess* (2nd century AD) describes her temple at Sidon and links her with the moon.
biblicalRole:
The plural Ashtaroth appears with Baal(s) as a pair for apostasy: Israel 'served the Baals and the Ashtaroth' (Judg 2:13; Judg 10:6), and Samuel calls Israel to put them away (1 Sam 7:3-4; 1 Sam 12:10). After killing Saul, the Philistines hang his armour in 'the house of Ashtaroth' (1 Sam 31:10), presumably at Beth-shan.

Solomon, influenced by his foreign wives, built high places on the hill east of Jerusalem for 'Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians', Chemosh of Moab and Milcom of Ammon (1 Kgs 11:5-7; 1 Kgs 11:33). They stood for more than three centuries, until Josiah defiled them. The narrator calls that hill 'the Mount of Corruption' (har ha-mashchit, 2 Kgs 23:13). This is very likely a pun on the Mount of Olives, which later Jewish texts call har ha-mishchah, 'Mount of Anointing' (from its olive oil); the pun is attractive but the 'Mount of Anointing' name is attested only later.

A town in Bashan was called Ashtaroth (Deut 1:4; Josh 12:4), presumably after her. She is also one of the candidates for the 'Queen of Heaven' of Jer 7 and 44 (debated).

encounters.title: The Baals and the Ashtaroth
encounters.summary: The pair 'Baals and Ashtaroth' stands for the whole Canaanite pantheon that Israel served in the time of the judges.

encounters.title: Saul's armour in the house of Ashtaroth
encounters.summary: The Philistines put Saul's armour in Ashtaroth's temple and fasten his body to the wall of Beth-shan, while 1 Chr 10:10 adds that his head went to Dagon's temple.

encounters.title: Solomon's shrine to Ashtoreth of the Sidonians
encounters.summary: Solomon follows Ashtoreth and builds high places for his wives' gods east of Jerusalem; God tears the kingdom from his son as a result.

encounters.title: Josiah defiles the Mount of Corruption
encounters.summary: Josiah defiles Solomon's shrines to Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom, breaks the pillars, cuts down the asherim and fills the places with human bones.

archaeology.find: Sarcophagi of Tabnit and Eshmunazar II
archaeology.place: Sidon, Lebanon (now Istanbul and the Louvre)
archaeology.summary: Phoenician royal coffins of the 6th-5th centuries BC. Tabnit calls himself 'priest of Astarte, king of the Sidonians'; Eshmunazar II says his mother Amotashtart was a priestess of Astarte and that the family built her temples in Sidon. They confirm the Bible's phrase 'Ashtoreth of the Sidonians'.
Gold sheets of c. 500 BC in Phoenician and Etruscan record a king's dedication of a shrine to Astarte, equated with the Etruscan goddess Uni. They show how far Phoenician traders carried her.
A large Phoenician temple, rebuilt over an older Bronze Age sanctuary, was dedicated to Astarte from the 9th century BC.

renamed.explanation: The Hebrew vowels of Ashtoreth (a-o-e) match those of bosheth, 'shame'. Most scholars since the 19th century think scribes deliberately read the goddess's name with the vowels of 'shame', just as they did with Baal names and probably Molech. The Greek form Astarte preserves the original vowels. A few scholars think the o-vowel could come from the plural Ashtaroth, so the case is strong but not certain.

laterFate: In Greek and Roman times she merged with Aphrodite and Venus Caelestis, and her Carthaginian counterpart became Juno Caelestis. In Christian demonology she changed gender: early modern grimoires such as Johann Weyer's *Pseudomonarchia Daemonum* (1577) and the *Lesser Key of Solomon* list 'Astaroth' as a great duke of hell, a male demon. Milton's *Paradise Lost* (Book 1) describes 'Astoreth', whom the Phoenicians called Astarte, queen of heaven with crescent horns, worshipped by Sidonian virgins under the moon.

name: Yam
symbol: raging sea; many-headed sea serpent

cultCenter.name: Ugarit (receives offerings in ritual lists; no known temple)

family.name: Lotan, the twisting serpent with seven heads

plain:
Yam is the Hebrew and Ugaritic word for 'sea', and at Ugarit it is also a god: the sea as a proud, threatening power that wants to rule. The storm god Baal defeats him.

The Bible does not worship Yam, but it borrows the picture: again and again Yahweh is the one who rebukes the sea, crushes the sea dragon and sets the sea its limits. When Jesus calms the storm and the disciples ask 'who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?', readers who know this background hear a claim about divine power.
myth: In the first part of the Baal Cycle, El makes Yam king and builds him a palace. Yam sends messengers to the divine assembly demanding that Baal be surrendered; the gods cower, and El agrees. Baal refuses. Kothar-wa-Khasis gives Baal two clubs, 'Driver' (Yagrush) and 'Chaser' (Aymur). The first strikes Yam's chest without effect; the second hits his head and he collapses. Astarte urges Baal to 'scatter' him, and Baal is hailed as king. Elsewhere Anat and Baal boast of having crushed 'Lotan the fleeing serpent, the twisting serpent, the mighty one with seven heads', Yam's monstrous partner.
biblicalRole:
The Hebrew word yam means the sea in thousands of ordinary verses, but in poetry the sea and its monsters are treated as hostile powers that God subdues. God 'divided the sea' and 'broke the heads of the dragons on the waters' and 'crushed the heads of Leviathan' (Ps 74:13-14); he 'rules the raging of the sea' and crushed Rahab (Ps 89:9-10; Job 26:12). Isaiah 27:1 promises God will punish 'Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent' and slay 'the dragon in the sea', wording that closely matches the Ugaritic description of Lotan.

The Bible's twist is that the sea is a creature, not a rival god: God set its bounds at creation (Job 38:8-11; Ps 104:9) and the dragons are his creatures (Gen 1:21; Ps 104:26). Scholars debate how far this is 'demythologising' Canaanite myth and how far it simply uses the region's poetic stock. The New Testament takes the picture to its end: Jesus rebukes the wind and sea (Mark 4:39-41), the beast rises from the sea (Rev 13:1), and in the new creation 'the sea was no more' (Rev 21:1).

encounters.title: God crushes the sea dragons
encounters.summary: Poetry praises God for dividing the sea and crushing Leviathan and Rahab, language that echoes Baal's victory over Yam.

encounters.title: Leviathan the twisting serpent
encounters.summary: Isaiah's phrase for the end-time defeat of evil almost matches the Ugaritic title of Yam's serpent ally Lotan.

encounters.title: The sea is given its limit
encounters.summary: God shut in the sea with doors and told it, 'Here your proud waves shall stop': the sea is a creature under command.

encounters.title: Jesus rebukes the sea
encounters.summary: Jesus rebukes the wind and says to the sea, 'Be still'; the disciples ask who this is that even the wind and sea obey him.

encounters.title: No more sea
encounters.summary: The beast rises from the sea, but in the new heaven and earth the sea is gone: chaos is finally removed.

archaeology.summary: The fragmentary first tablets of the Baal Cycle tell the conflict between Baal and Yam.
Mot reminds Baal that he struck 'Lotan the fleeing serpent, the twisting serpent, the powerful one with seven heads', wording parallel to Isa 27:1.

laterFate: Yam was never a major cult god and vanished with Ugarit. The image of the sea-monster survived as Leviathan, who became a symbol of chaos in Jewish apocalyptic (to be served at the messianic banquet in later Jewish tradition) and gave Thomas Hobbes the title of his 1651 book on the state.

name: Mot
symbol: an enormous open mouth swallowing everything; a city of mud and filth

cultCenter.name: Ugarit (no known temple; myth places his city, Hmry, in the underworld)

plain:
Mot is death itself, pictured as a god with a bottomless appetite. In the Baal Cycle he swallows the storm god Baal, and the world dries out until Baal returns.

In Hebrew mot (mavet) is simply the word for death, and nobody in the Bible worships it. But the prophets and psalmists use the same picture of Death as a greedy swallower, and then reverse it: one day God will 'swallow up death for ever' (Isa 25:8), a line Paul quotes about the resurrection.
myth: Mot's mouth stretches from earth to sky, one lip to heaven, one to the underworld, and his throat swallows like a lion or a camel. Baal, newly enthroned, sends him a message that he alone is king; Mot replies with a threat and invites Baal to eat with him. Baal submits, descends into Mot's throat and dies. Anat later seizes Mot, splits, winnows, burns, grinds and sows him like grain. Yet Mot is back seven years later to fight Baal until the sun goddess Shapash warns him that El will overturn his throne, and he yields.
biblicalRole:
Death in the Bible is never a god to be worshipped, but it is sometimes personified in ways that echo Mot. Death is greedy and never satisfied (Hab 2:5; Prov 27:20); it 'has come up into our windows' (Jer 9:21), a line some connect with Baal's hesitation over a window in his palace (debated). Sheol 'opens its mouth beyond measure' (Isa 5:14). Hosea taunts: 'O Death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your sting?' (Hos 13:14).

The decisive reversal is Isa 25:8: on God's mountain he 'will swallow up death for ever'. The swallower is swallowed. Paul quotes Isaiah and Hosea together for the resurrection (1 Cor 15:54-55), and Revelation pictures Death and Hades thrown into the lake of fire (Rev 20:14). Whether the biblical writers knew Mot as a mythic figure or simply used natural personification is debated; the parallels in imagery are clear.

encounters.title: Death comes through the windows
encounters.summary: Jeremiah pictures death climbing into houses and cutting off children from the streets.

encounters.title: Death's open mouth
encounters.summary: Sheol and Death are described as an insatiable mouth, the same image as Mot's throat.

encounters.title: God will swallow up death
encounters.summary: In Isaiah's vision of the feast on Zion, God swallows Death for ever and wipes away tears.

encounters.title: Where is your sting?
encounters.summary: Hosea's taunt to Death becomes Paul's victory cry over death in the resurrection.

encounters.title: Death thrown into the lake of fire
encounters.summary: Death is the last enemy to be destroyed.

archaeology.summary: Tell the conflict between Baal and Mot, Baal's death and return, and Anat's destruction of Mot.

laterFate: Mot had no cult to continue. Philo of Byblos (via Eusebius) mentions a 'Muth' whom the Phoenicians called Death and Pluto. The personified Death of Christian art, the rider on the pale horse (Rev 6:8) and the later Grim Reaper, owe more to the Bible and medieval imagination than to Ugarit, though the family resemblance is real.

name: Kothar-wa-Khasis
symbol: smith's tools: hammer, tongs and bellows

cultCenter.name: Ugarit (myth places his home at Kaphtor, probably Crete, and Hikuptah, Memphis in Egypt)

family.relation: birth goddesses with a related name (possibly)
family.name: the Kotharat

plain:
Kothar-wa-Khasis, 'Skilful-and-Wise', is the Canaanite craftsman god: the divine smith and architect. He makes Baal's weapons and builds his palace.

He is never mentioned in the Bible. He matters to Bible readers mainly because his stories show how people of the time thought about temples: a god's house had to be built by a divinely gifted craftsman. The Bible tells similar stories of human craftsmen filled with God's Spirit and skill: Bezalel for the tabernacle and Hiram of Tyre for Solomon's temple.
myth: Kothar lives far away in Kaphtor (probably Crete) and in Hikuptah (Memphis, Egypt), places famous for fine crafts. He forges the two clubs, 'Driver' and 'Chaser', with which Baal defeats Yam. He builds Baal's palace on Zaphon with a seven-day fire that turns silver and gold into bricks. He argues that the palace should have a window, which Baal at first refuses and later accepts. In the Aqhat epic he makes the beautiful bow that Anat covets. He also appears in incantations as a spell-maker.
biblicalRole: No biblical text names Kothar. Possible echoes are indirect: the Philistines are said to come from Caphtor (Amos 9:7; Jer 47:4), the same place-name as Kothar's home; and the Bible's craftsmen are filled with wisdom and skill to build God's dwelling (Bezalel in Exod 31:2-5; Hiram of Tyre, a Phoenician bronze-worker, in 1 Kgs 7:13-14). Some scholars also hear the related Kotharat (birth goddesses) behind the rare word kosharot ('prosperity') in Ps 68:6. These links are suggestive, not proven. The biblical point, in contrast with Ugarit, is that skill itself is God's gift to human workers.

encounters.title: Bezalel filled with skill
encounters.summary: God fills Bezalel with his Spirit, wisdom and craftsmanship to build the tabernacle: a human craftsman, not a craftsman god.

encounters.title: Hiram of Tyre builds Solomon's bronzework
encounters.summary: A Phoenician master-craftsman, 'full of wisdom, understanding and skill', makes the temple's bronze pillars and furnishings.

encounters.title: Caphtor
encounters.summary: Caphtor, probably Crete, is named as the Philistines' place of origin; Ugarit calls it Kothar's home.

archaeology.summary: Describe Kothar making Baal's clubs and building his palace.

archaeology.find: Philo of Byblos, *Phoenician History* (quoted by Eusebius)
archaeology.year: written c. AD 100; preserved in the 4th century
archaeology.summary: Philo describes 'Chousor', inventor of iron-working, spells and fishing tackle, and equates him with the Greek smith-god Hephaestus: a late echo of Kothar.

laterFate: Kothar's memory faded into Philo of Byblos's 'Chousor', equated with Hephaestus. He plays no role in Jewish or Christian demonology.

name: Resheph
original: Ugaritic and Phoenician rshp; Hebrew reshep ('flame, plague')
symbol: smiting warrior with mace and shield, wearing a crown with a gazelle's head; arrows

cultCenter.name: Kition, Cyprus (Resheph-Mikal); also worshipped at Ebla, Ugarit and in New Kingdom Egypt

family.relation: fellow member of the Ugaritic pantheon
family.name: Baal-Hadad

plain:
Resheph was the god of plague and of war, an archer whose arrows brought disease. He was worshipped across the Near East for some two thousand years, from Ebla in Syria to Egypt and Cyprus.

In the Bible his name is a common word meaning 'flame', 'fiery bolt' or 'plague'. In a few poems, though, resheph seems to be pictured as a person: in Habakkuk 3:5, 'plague went before him, and resheph went out at his feet', as if the old plague god now marches as a servant in Yahweh's procession.
myth: Resheph's myths are poorly preserved. At Ugarit he is the gatekeeper of the sun goddess and a god of plague; in the Kirta epic he carries off a fifth of the king's family. In Egypt, Pharaoh Amenhotep II and later kings honoured him as a war god, and stelae show him with a mace, shield and a gazelle-headed crown. In Cyprus he was called 'Resheph of the arrow' and identified with Apollo, the Greek archer-god who also sent plague.
biblicalRole:
Resheph appears as a common noun in several poems, sometimes with personal colouring: God threatens Israel with 'hunger, burning heat (resheph) and bitter pestilence' (Deut 32:24); 'plague went before him, and resheph followed at his feet' (Hab 3:5); God gave Egypt's flocks 'to reshaphim', fiery bolts (Ps 78:48); he broke 'the reshaphim of the bow', flashing arrows (Ps 76:3); love's flashes are 'flashes (reshaphim) of fire' (Song 8:6); and humans are born to trouble as 'the sons of resheph fly upward', sparks or perhaps birds (Job 5:7). A descendant of Ephraim is also called Resheph (1 Chr 7:25).

Most scholars read Hab 3:5 and Deut 32:24 as demoted deities: once-feared gods now reduced to forces in Yahweh's service. Others see only poetic personification of plague. Either way the theology is that disease is not an independent divine power.

encounters.title: Plague and Resheph march with God
encounters.summary: In Habakkuk's storm-theophany, Pestilence goes before God and Resheph follows at his feet, like attendants in a royal procession.

encounters.title: Burning plague as covenant curse
encounters.summary: God threatens to send 'arrows' and 'resheph' against faithless Israel, the vocabulary of the archer plague god.

encounters.title: Fiery bolts and arrows
encounters.summary: Resheph as a common noun for flames, lightning, flaming arrows and sparks.

archaeology.summary: Mid-3rd-millennium BC texts list Rashap among the gods with his own temple and gate, showing his great age.
New Kingdom stelae show Resheph as a smiting warrior with a gazelle-headed crown, worshipped by Egyptians and foreigners.
A 4th-century BC Phoenician-Greek dedication equates Resheph with Apollo.

laterFate: Through Cyprus Resheph merged into Apollo. In Hebrew the word survived only as 'flame' or 'spark' (modern Hebrew reshef). He has no role in Milton or in Christian demonology.

name: Dagon
original: Hebrew dagon; Akkadian and Ugaritic dagan
domains: the dead and funerary offerings (at Ugarit and Mari)
symbol: ears of grain; an enthroned father god (not a fish, despite the popular image)

cultCenter.name: Ashdod (Philistine temple of Dagon); also Gaza; earlier Tuttul and Terqa on the middle Euphrates

plain:
Dagon was the chief god of the Philistines in the Bible, with temples at Ashdod and Gaza. He is famous for falling flat on his face in front of the Ark of the Covenant.

One common myth needs correcting: Dagon was not a fish god. The idea arose because the Hebrew word dag means 'fish', and medieval Jewish commentators such as David Kimhi imagined an idol that was half man, half fish; Milton then made it famous. In fact Dagan was an old Syrian grain god (dagan is Hebrew for 'grain'), worshipped at Ebla and Mari a thousand years before the Philistines arrived. The Philistines, who came from the Aegean world, adopted him when they settled in Canaan.
myth: No myth about Dagan survives. Texts from the 3rd and 2nd millennia BC show him as a great god of the middle Euphrates: 'Lord of the Land', giver of grain, and a god of oracles and kingship. Sargon of Akkad (c. 2300 BC) records that he bowed down to Dagan at Tuttul, who gave him the 'upper land' as far as the Cedar Forest. At Mari prophets delivered oracles in his name, and he received offerings for the dead. At Ugarit he had a temple beside Baal's, and Baal is repeatedly called 'son of Dagan', though in the myths Baal belongs to El's family. Philo of Byblos later explained Dagon as 'Siton', grain, and credited him with inventing the plough.
biblicalRole:
Dagon appears in three scenes.

1. Samson's death (Judg 16:23-30). The Philistine lords gather in Dagon's temple at Gaza to celebrate that 'our god has given Samson our enemy into our hand'. Samson pushes apart the two central pillars and the house falls on them.

2. The ark at Ashdod (1 Sam 5). After capturing the Ark of the Covenant (c. 1050 BC on the usual chronology), the Philistines set it in Dagon's temple as a trophy beside their god. Next morning Dagon lies face down before the ark. They set him up again; the next morning he has fallen again, and his head and both hands lie cut off on the threshold, and 'only Dagon was left to him', an odd phrase usually taken to mean only his trunk or body. That is why, says the narrator, Dagon's priests do not step on the threshold 'to this day' (1 Sam 5:5; compare Zeph 1:9, those who 'leap over the threshold'). A plague of 'tumours' (ophalim, swellings; the Hebrew margin reads tehorim) breaks out in Ashdod, Gath and Ekron. They might be buboes of bubonic plague, haemorrhoids, or a genital affliction; it is debated. The Philistines return the ark with five golden tumours and five golden mice (1 Sam 6:4-5), and the mice have suggested to many a rodent-borne plague (the Greek Septuagint adds mice already in 1 Sam 5:6).

3. Saul's head (1 Chr 10:10). After Saul's death on Gilboa, the Philistines fasten his head in the temple of Dagon, while his armour goes to the house of Ashtaroth and his body hangs on the wall of Beth-shan (1 Sam 31:10).

The ark story is a 'battle of the gods' told with mockery: the defeated people's God humiliates the victors' god in his own house.

encounters.title: Samson brings down Dagon's temple at Gaza
encounters.summary: The Philistines praise Dagon for capturing Samson; Samson pulls down the pillars and kills more in his death than in his life.

encounters.title: Dagon falls before the ark at Ashdod
encounters.summary: Dagon falls face down before the ark, then is found with head and hands broken off on the threshold.

encounters.title: Tumours and mice; the ark sent back
encounters.summary: Plague spreads through the Philistine cities; the ark is returned on a new cart with golden tumours and golden mice as a guilt offering.

encounters.title: Saul's head in Dagon's temple
encounters.summary: The Philistines display Saul's head in Dagon's temple and his armour in the temple of Ashtaroth.

encounters.title: Leaping over the threshold
encounters.summary: Zephaniah condemns those who 'leap over the threshold', possibly a custom like that of Dagon's priests.

encounters.title: Place names Beth-dagon
encounters.summary: Two towns called Beth-dagon ('house of Dagon') show the god was known in Canaan before or alongside the Philistines.

archaeology.place: Tell Hariri (Mari) and Tell Mardikh (Ebla), Syria
archaeology.summary: 3rd- and 2nd-millennium BC archives show Dagan as a major god of the middle Euphrates, with prophets speaking in his name at Mari.

archaeology.find: Temple of Dagan and dedicatory stelae
archaeology.summary: One of the two temples on Ugarit's acropolis has been identified as Dagan's on the basis of two stelae recording offerings to him; the identification is widely but not universally accepted.
Excavations revealed a major Philistine city with Aegean-style pottery and cult figurines (including the 'Ashdoda' seated goddess), but Dagon's temple itself has not been found.

archaeology.year: excavations at Ashkelon, Ekron, Ashdod; ancient DNA study 2019
archaeology.summary: Pottery, architecture and a 2019 DNA study from Ashkelon point to a European/Aegean origin for the first Philistines in the 12th century BC, who soon mixed with locals. This supports the view that they adopted Dagan from their Semitic neighbours.

laterFate: Dagon's temple at Ashdod was still standing in the 2nd century BC, when, according to 1 Maccabees 10, the Hasmonean leader Jonathan burned it with those who had fled inside. The fish-god idea came from medieval Jewish commentators playing on dag ('fish') and was cemented by Milton's *Paradise Lost* (Book 1), which describes Dagon as a 'sea monster', man above and fish below, mourning in his own temple when the ark maimed him. Later 'fish-god' images of Dagon draw on Assyrian reliefs of fish-cloaked apkallu sages, which have nothing to do with him. H. P. Lovecraft's 1919 story 'Dagon' turned him into a sea deity of horror fiction.

name: Baal-zebub
domains: oracles and healing (as consulted by Ahaziah)
probably a local form of Baal the storm god
symbol: flies (by the biblical pun); otherwise the storm god's emblems

cultCenter.name: Ekron (Tel Miqne)

plain:
Baal-zebub was the god of the Philistine city of Ekron, whom King Ahaziah of Israel tried to consult when he was injured. The name as written means 'Lord of Flies'.

Most scholars think that is a deliberate insult. At Ugarit Baal is often called zbl b'l, 'Prince Baal', so the god's real title was probably Baal-zebul, 'Baal the Prince' or 'Lord of the exalted house'. Changing one letter turned 'Lord Prince' into 'Lord of Flies'. By the time of Jesus 'Beelzebul' had become a name for the prince of demons.
myth: No myth of Ekron's god survives. If he was a local Baal, his worshippers will have told the storm god's stories: Baal the Prince (zbl), who defeats Sea, dies and returns. Ahaziah's embassy suggests Ekron's temple had a reputation as an oracle where one could ask about healing. A minority view takes 'lord of flies' at face value: a god who could drive away (or send) flies and the diseases they carried, comparable to the Greek 'Zeus Apomyios', 'Zeus who averts flies'.
biblicalRole:
King Ahaziah of Israel, son of Ahab, falls through the lattice of his upper room in Samaria and sends messengers to ask Baal-zebub, god of Ekron, whether he will recover. Elijah intercepts them with a question that becomes the theme of the story: 'Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are going to inquire of Baal-zebub?' Ahaziah dies as Elijah predicted (2 Kgs 1:2-17).

In the Gospels, opponents accuse Jesus of driving out demons 'by Beelzebul, the prince of demons' (Matt 12:24; Mark 3:22; Luke 11:15). Jesus answers that a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand, and that if he casts out demons by the Spirit (finger) of God, the kingdom of God has come. He also says that if they called the master of the house Beelzebul, they will malign his household too (Matt 10:25), which may play on zebul as 'house'. The Greek manuscripts read Beelzeboul; the Latin Vulgate and Syriac tradition read Beelzebub, which is why the KJV has 'Beelzebub'.

encounters.title: Ahaziah sends to Baal-zebub
encounters.summary: The injured king seeks an oracle from Ekron's god; Elijah asks, 'Is there no God in Israel?'

encounters.title: Fire on the captains
encounters.summary: Fire falls on two companies sent to seize Elijah; he then goes to Ahaziah and repeats the verdict in person.

encounters.title: Ahaziah dies
encounters.summary: The king dies according to Elijah's word.

encounters.title: Jesus accused of using Beelzebul
encounters.summary: Opponents say Jesus casts out demons by Beelzebul, prince of demons. Jesus replies with the divided-kingdom saying and the binding of the strong man.

encounters.title: The master of the house called Beelzebul
encounters.summary: Jesus warns his disciples that if he was slandered as Beelzebul, they will be too.

archaeology.summary: Baal is repeatedly called 'Prince, Lord of the earth' (zbl b'l ars). This is the main evidence that the original name was Baal-zebul and that 'zebub' is a deliberate change.
The 7th-century BC temple inscription from Ekron names the goddess Ptgyh, not Baal-zebub, so Ekron's pantheon is still only partly known.

renamed.original: Baal-zebul, 'Baal the Prince' or 'Lord of the (exalted) dwelling'
renamed.explanation: A one-letter change (final l to b) turns an honorific into a sneer. The New Testament form Beelzebul preserves the l, suggesting the original was remembered. A minority of scholars think 'Lord of flies' was the god's real title, perhaps for a healing god who drove away flies.

laterFate: Beelzebub became one of the great names of Christian demonology: the prince of demons, sometimes identified with Satan and sometimes ranked just below him. In the *Testament of Solomon* (early centuries AD) 'Beelzeboul' is the prince of demons questioned by Solomon. Milton's *Paradise Lost* (Book 1) makes Beelzebub Satan's chief lieutenant, next to him in power and crime, who wakes beside him on the burning lake. He appears in medieval mystery plays, in Marlowe's *Doctor Faustus*, and gave William Golding's novel *Lord of the Flies* (1954) its title.

name: Baal-peor
domains: feasting and sexual rites (as the Bible describes his worship)
symbol: no known image; a mountain shrine

cultCenter.name: Beth-peor, on the plains of Moab near Mount Nebo (exact site uncertain)

plain:
Baal-peor was 'the lord of Peor', a local god worshipped at a mountain shrine in Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho. Israel's first great fall into idolatry, just before entering the promised land, happened there.

The story became a byword. For centuries afterwards prophets, psalmists and apostles remembered 'what happened at Peor' as the warning example of how quickly God's people could abandon him.
myth: Nothing is known of this god apart from the Bible. Most scholars think he was a local form of Baal (or of Chemosh) worshipped at Mount Peor. Psalm 106:28 says Israel 'ate sacrifices offered to the dead', which has led some scholars to link the cult with the marzeah, a feast for the dead known from Ugarit and later texts; others take 'the dead' as a jibe at lifeless idols.
biblicalRole:
While Israel camped at Shittim, the people 'began to whore with the daughters of Moab', ate at their sacrificial meals, bowed to their gods and 'yoked themselves to Baal of Peor' (Num 25:1-3). A plague broke out; Phinehas the priest ended it by spearing an Israelite man and a Midianite woman in the act. 24,000 died (Num 25:9; Paul gives 23,000 in 1 Cor 10:8, perhaps counting a single day or using a round figure). Numbers later blames Balaam's advice for the seduction (Num 31:16).

The event became a standard warning: Deut 4:3; Josh 22:17 ('is the iniquity of Peor too little for us?'); Hos 9:10 ('they came to Baal-peor and consecrated themselves to the shame'); Ps 106:28-31; 1 Cor 10:8; Rev 2:14.

encounters.title: Israel yokes itself to Baal-peor
encounters.summary: Israelites join Moabite feasts and worship; Moses orders the leaders of the apostasy executed.

encounters.title: Phinehas stops the plague
encounters.summary: Phinehas kills Zimri and the Midianite Cozbi; the plague stops after 24,000 deaths, and Phinehas receives a covenant of priesthood.

encounters.title: Balaam's counsel
encounters.summary: The seduction at Peor is traced to Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before Israel.

encounters.title: Remembered for centuries
encounters.summary: Peor becomes shorthand for apostasy; Hosea says Israel became as detestable as what it loved.

encounters.title: Paul's warning
encounters.summary: Paul cites the fall of 23,000 in one day as a warning to the Corinthians against sexual immorality and idol feasts.

archaeology.summary: A c. 800 BC text about 'Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods' shows that Balaam was a remembered figure in Transjordan, the region of the Peor story. It does not mention Peor.

laterFate: Rabbinic tradition (e.g. the Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 64a) claimed that Peor was worshipped by exposing oneself and defecating before the idol, a crude tradition with no ancient support. Milton's *Paradise Lost* (Book 1) gives 'Peor' as another name of Chemosh, the obscene dread of Moab. Renaissance demonology turned him into Belphegor, a demon of sloth and ingenious invention, the hero of Machiavelli's comic tale *Belfagor arcidiavolo*.

name: Baal-berith
symbol: temple-fortress and standing stone at Shechem

cultCenter.name: Shechem (Tell Balata, near Nablus)

plain:
Baal-berith, 'Lord of the Covenant', was the god of the old Canaanite city of Shechem. After Gideon died, the Israelites 'made Baal-berith their god', and his temple funded the bloody rise of Gideon's son Abimelech.

The name is striking because Shechem was also where Joshua renewed Israel's covenant with Yahweh. So the city had two 'covenant' traditions side by side, and the Bible tells how one was swapped for the other.
myth: No myth survives. He is called both Baal-berith (Judg 8:33; Judg 9:4) and El-berith (Judg 9:46), so scholars debate whether he was a form of El, a form of Baal, or a title used for both. 'Lord of the Covenant' probably means the god who guaranteed treaties sworn in his temple, perhaps a treaty between Shechem's Canaanites and neighbouring Israelite clans.
biblicalRole:
Shechem was already an old sacred site in Genesis: Abraham's first altar in Canaan (Gen 12:6-7) and Jacob's purchase of land and altar there (Gen 33:18-20). Joshua made a covenant with Israel at Shechem and set up a great stone under the oak by the sanctuary (Josh 24:25-26).

After Gideon's death, the Israelites again served the Baals and made Baal-berith their god (Judg 8:33). The Shechemites gave Abimelech 70 pieces of silver from Baal-berith's temple, with which he hired 'worthless and reckless men' and murdered his 70 brothers (Judg 9:4-5). When Abimelech later turned on Shechem, about a thousand people took refuge in the stronghold of the temple of El-berith; he set it on fire and they all died (Judg 9:46-49).

encounters.title: Israel makes Baal-berith its god
encounters.summary: As soon as Gideon dies, Israel forgets Yahweh and adopts Shechem's covenant god.

encounters.title: Temple silver funds a massacre
encounters.summary: Seventy shekels from Baal-berith's temple pay for Abimelech's hired men, who kill his brothers; Abimelech is made king by the oak at Shechem.

encounters.title: The tower of El-berith burns
encounters.summary: Abimelech burns the stronghold of El-berith's temple with a thousand men and women inside.

encounters.title: Joshua's covenant at Shechem
encounters.summary: Earlier at the same place, Joshua had made Israel's covenant with Yahweh and set up a witness stone.

archaeology.year: 1926 (Ernst Sellin); 1956-1973 (G. Ernest Wright and the Drew-McCormick expedition)
archaeology.summary: A massive temple with walls about 5 m thick, built in the Middle Bronze Age and reused into the Late Bronze or early Iron Age, with a large standing stone in its forecourt. Wright identified it with the 'house of El-berith' of Judges 9. The identification is popular but debated, especially regarding whether the building was still in use at the time of Abimelech.

laterFate: In early modern demonology 'Berith' (or Baalberith) appears as a demon: a duke of hell in the *Lesser Key of Solomon*, and a demon named during the Aix-en-Provence possession case of 1610-1611. These lists borrowed biblical names freely and have no connection with ancient Shechem.

name: Ptgyh
domains: patron goddess of the royal temple of Ekron
symbol: unknown; only the name survives

cultCenter.name: Ekron (Tel Miqne), temple complex 650

plain:
Ptgyh is a goddess known from just one inscription: the royal dedication stone found at Ekron, one of the five Philistine cities, in 1996. The king of Ekron says he built the temple for 'Ptgyh his lady'.

Nobody knows who she was. The Bible never mentions her. She is a useful reminder that the Bible names only a few of the gods its neighbours worshipped, and that archaeology keeps turning up new ones.
myth: No myth is known. Because the Philistines came from the Aegean world, several scholars have proposed that Ptgyh is a Greek goddess written in Semitic letters: suggestions include Pythogaia (an earth goddess linked with Delphi), Potnia ('Lady', a title of Aegean goddesses) or a form of Gaia. None of these is proven.
biblicalRole: Ptgyh is not mentioned in the Bible. The inscription is valuable because its kings are known from both Assyrian records and, by name type, the Bible. King Ikausu son of Padi is mentioned in the annals of the Assyrian kings Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal (early 7th century BC); his father Padi appears in Sennacherib's account of his 701 BC campaign, the same campaign described in 2 Kgs 18-19. The name Ikausu is generally thought to be the same as Achish, the name of the Philistine king of Gath whom David served (1 Sam 27:2), and may mean 'the Achaean' (Greek).

encounters.title: Ekron among the Philistine cities
encounters.summary: Ekron is one of the five Philistine cities that received the ark; its later temple belonged to Ptgyh.

encounters.title: Achish, a Philistine royal name
encounters.summary: David serves Achish king of Gath. The same name (Ikausu) appears centuries later for a king of Ekron in the Ptgyh inscription.

encounters.title: Prophecies against Ekron
encounters.summary: The prophets announce judgement on Ekron along with the other Philistine cities; Ekron was destroyed by Babylon in 604 BC.

archaeology.summary: A five-line limestone block, found in situ in a large temple, reads in substance: the house that Ikausu son of Padi, son of Ysd, son of Ada, son of Ya'ir, ruler of Ekron, built for Ptgyh his lady; may she bless him, protect him, prolong his days and bless his land. It confirms the Assyrian-attested kings and that Ekron was named Ekron, and is a key text for Philistine religion. The goddess's identity remains unknown.
Proposals include Pythogaia, Potnia or a Greek-derived goddess, reflecting the Philistines' Aegean roots; others suggest a local Semitic goddess. Unresolved.

laterFate: Ptgyh vanished with Ekron's destruction by Nebuchadnezzar in 604 BC and was unknown until 1996.

name: Molech
otherNames: possibly Malik / Milku (Syrian and Mesopotamian underworld god)
original: Hebrew ha-molek (always with the article 'the' except once); consonants mlk = 'king'
domains: child sacrifice by fire ('passing through the fire')
possibly the underworld and the dead
symbol: fire pit (topheth); later imagined as a bull-headed bronze statue with outstretched arms

cultCenter.name: Topheth in the Valley of Ben-Hinnom, south of Jerusalem

family.relation: compared with the Carthaginian cult of
family.name: Baal Hammon

plain:
Molech is the name the Bible links with the worst practice it condemns: making children 'pass through the fire', that is, burning them as sacrifices, at a place called Topheth in the valley just south of Jerusalem.

There is a real scholarly argument about whether Molech was a god at all. The consonants mlk mean 'king'. Many scholars think the vowels were changed to those of bosheth, 'shame', turning melek ('king') into molek. Others, following Otto Eissfeldt (1935), argue that molk was a Phoenician word for a type of sacrifice, so 'to Molech' originally meant 'as a molk-offering'. Others again argue that Molech was a real underworld god. What no one disputes is that the Bible describes child sacrifice in Judah and condemns it in the strongest terms.
myth: No myth of a god called Molech survives. If he was a god, the best candidate is Malik or Milku, a god of the underworld and the dead attested at Ebla, Mari and Ugarit, where one text places 'Milku' at Ashtaroth in Bashan. The famous picture of Moloch as a hollow bronze idol with a bull's head, heated red-hot, with children placed in its arms while drums drowned out the cries, comes from medieval Jewish commentaries (e.g. Rashi on Jer 7:31, explaining the name Topheth from toph, 'drum') and from Greek stories about Carthage, not from the Bible or any ancient Israelite source.
biblicalRole:
The law forbids giving any child 'to Molech' on pain of death (Lev 18:21; Lev 20:2-5) and forbids making a child 'pass through the fire' (Deut 18:10). Despite this, two kings of Judah did it: Ahaz 'made his son pass through the fire' (2 Kgs 16:3) and Manasseh did the same (2 Kgs 21:6). Topheth in the Valley of Ben-Hinnom was the site (Jer 7:31; Jer 32:35). God says through Jeremiah that it was something 'I did not command, nor did it come into my mind' (Jer 7:31; Jer 19:5). Josiah defiled Topheth so that no one could use it again (2 Kgs 23:10), probably around 622 BC.

Solomon is said to have built a high place for 'Molech the abomination of the Ammonites' (1 Kgs 11:7), whereas two verses earlier the Ammonite god is Milcom (1 Kgs 11:5). This suggests either that the two names were confused or that the writer treated Milcom and Molech as the same 'king' god.

The Valley of Hinnom (ge hinnom) became, through its association with burning and judgement (Jer 7:32; Jer 19:6), the name Gehenna, the word Jesus uses for the place of final judgement (eleven times in the Gospels, e.g. Matt 5:22; Mark 9:43). Stephen, quoting the Greek of Amos 5:26, mentions 'the tent of Moloch' (Acts 7:43); the Hebrew of Amos reads 'Sakkuth your king' at that point.

encounters.summary: Anyone who gives a child to Molech is to be put to death; the practice profanes God's name.

encounters.summary: Two kings of Judah make their sons pass through the fire, 'according to the abominations of the nations'.

encounters.summary: Josiah ruins Topheth so that no one can again burn a son or daughter there to Molech.

encounters.title: 'Which I did not command'
encounters.summary: Jeremiah condemns the high places of Topheth and renames the valley 'the Valley of Slaughter'.

encounters.title: Gehenna in the teaching of Jesus

encounters.summary: Stephen quotes the Greek version of Amos to accuse Israel of carrying the tent of Moloch in the wilderness.

archaeology.summary: Stelae from Carthage and other Punic sites use mlk as a sacrifice term (mlk 'mr, 'molk of a lamb'; mlk b'l, of uncertain meaning). Otto Eissfeldt argued that biblical 'to Molech' meant 'as a molk-sacrifice'. Many accepted this; George Heider (1985) and John Day (1989) argued strongly for a real deity Molek. The debate continues.

archaeology.find: Ugaritic mention of Milku at Ashtaroth
archaeology.summary: Ritual and snake-bite incantation texts mention a god mlk dwelling at 'ttrt (Ashtaroth), connected with the dead (the rpum, Rephaim). Supporters of a real god Molech cite this.

A sacred precinct with thousands of urns of burned infants and young animals under stelae to Baal Hammon and Tanit, often used as a parallel for Jerusalem's Topheth. Whether it shows routine child sacrifice is debated (see Baal Hammon and Tanit).

No sacrificial precinct like Carthage's has been found in the Hinnom valley; the valley has many tombs (including the Ketef Hinnom tombs with the silver amulet blessing). Topheth's exact location is unknown.

renamed.original: melek, 'king' (as a divine title), or molk, a sacrifice term
renamed.explanation: Since Abraham Geiger (1857) many scholars have argued that the vowels o-e were taken from bosheth, 'shame', as with Ashtoreth and the Baal names. Eissfeldt's alternative explains the form as a genuine Phoenician sacrificial term. A third view takes Molek as a genuine divine name (compare Malik). The Greek Septuagint sometimes translates it as 'ruler' or 'king', showing that early readers did not all read it as a proper name.

laterFate: Moloch became the archetype of a god who devours children. Milton's *Paradise Lost* (Book 1) puts Moloch first in the catalogue of fallen angels: a horrid king smeared with the blood of human sacrifice and parents' tears, worshipped by the Ammonites with drums drowning the children's cries. In modern culture Moloch stands for any system that consumes people: the machine in Fritz Lang's film *Metropolis* (1927) and the 'Moloch' section of Allen Ginsberg's poem *Howl* (1956).

name: Milcom
symbol: crowned king (a heavy gold crown in 2 Sam 12:30, if the crown is the god's)

cultCenter.name: Rabbah of the Ammonites (Amman Citadel, Jordan)

plain:
Milcom was the national god of the Ammonites, whose capital Rabbah lies under modern Amman in Jordan. His name comes from melek, 'king'. Solomon built him a shrine on the hill east of Jerusalem, which stood until Josiah tore it down.

Because Milcom and Molech share the same root letters, the Bible itself sometimes seems to mix them up, and scholars still debate whether they were one god or two. The best evidence is that Milcom was Ammon's ordinary state god, while 'Molech' is linked mainly with child sacrifice in Jerusalem.
myth: No Ammonite myths survive. Ammonite personal names and seals show a people who worshipped Milcom alongside El and others, much as Moabites worshipped Chemosh and Judahites Yahweh. A national god was the divine king of the land: he gave it to his people and fought their wars.
biblicalRole:
Solomon 'went after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites' and built a high place for him (1 Kgs 11:5; 1 Kgs 11:33); Josiah defiled it centuries later (2 Kgs 23:13). Zephaniah condemns those who swear by Yahweh and also by Milcom (Zeph 1:5, Masoretic 'Malcam'). Jeremiah asks why 'Milcom' has dispossessed Gad and his people settle in its cities, and announces that Milcom will go into exile with his priests (Jer 49:1; Jer 49:3).

When David captured Rabbah he took 'the crown of their king' (malkam), weighing a talent of gold, and it was placed on David's head (2 Sam 12:30). A talent (around 30 kg) is too heavy for a human king to wear, so many (following the Greek Septuagint, which reads 'Milcom their king') think it was the crown of Milcom's statue, perhaps with its precious stone set in David's crown. This is a plausible reading, not a certain one.

1 Kings 11:7 calls the Ammonite god 'Molech', raising the question whether Milcom and Molech were the same. Most scholars now treat them as distinct, explaining 11:7 as a scribal slip or a deliberate slur.

encounters.title: David takes the crown at Rabbah
encounters.summary: David captures the Ammonite capital and takes a crown of a talent of gold, probably from Milcom's image (debated).

encounters.summary: Solomon worships Milcom and builds his shrine east of Jerusalem.

encounters.title: Josiah defiles it
encounters.summary: Josiah defiles the high places Solomon built for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom on the Mount of Corruption.

encounters.title: Swearing by Yahweh and by Milcom
encounters.summary: Zephaniah condemns those who mix oaths by Yahweh with oaths by Milcom.

encounters.title: Milcom goes into exile
encounters.summary: Jeremiah mocks the god whose people took Gad's land: Milcom and his priests will go into captivity.

archaeology.summary: A fragmentary 9th-century BC Ammonite building inscription that begins with the word mlkm, usually read as Milcom speaking or being invoked. The reading of the rest is uncertain.

archaeology.find: Seal impression of an official of Baalis
archaeology.summary: A clay seal impression reads 'belonging to Milkom'ur, servant of Ba'alyasha'. Ba'alyasha is very likely Baalis, the Ammonite king who plotted Gedaliah's murder (Jer 40:14). Milkom'ur ('Milcom is light') shows the god's name in everyday use.
Many Ammonite seals carry names with Milcom; limestone statues of bearded men from Amman may show kings or the god himself (debated).

renamed.biblical: malkam, 'their king' (Masoretic vowels in 2 Sam 12:30, Jer 49:1, Jer 49:3, Zeph 1:5)
renamed.explanation: The same Hebrew consonants mlkm can be read as the god's name Milcom or as malkam, 'their king'. The Masoretic vowels often give 'their king' where the Greek Septuagint read 'Milcom'. Whether this was a deliberate way of avoiding the god's name or an honest ambiguity is debated; modern translations often restore Milcom.

laterFate: Ammon was absorbed by Babylon and later empires, and Milcom's worship faded. Milton's *Paradise Lost* (Book 1) does not list Milcom separately but places Moloch's worship among 'the Ammonite' in Rabbah, following 1 Kgs 11:7 in treating them as one.

name: Chemosh
domains: divine anger and favour toward his people
symbol: no certain image; a warrior god known from the Mesha Stele

cultCenter.name: Dibon (Dhiban, Jordan), Mesha's capital and the find-site of the Mesha Stele

family.name: Ashtar, probably a male form of Astarte

plain:
Chemosh was the national god of Moab, the kingdom east of the Dead Sea. The Moabites were 'the people of Chemosh' just as Israel was the people of Yahweh.

Chemosh is the one neighbouring god whose own worshippers' voice we can still hear clearly, thanks to the Mesha Stele, an inscription of about 840 BC in which King Mesha of Moab explains his country's history in exactly the terms the book of Kings uses for Israel: his god was angry and let the enemy oppress the land, then his god said 'Go!' and gave him victory.
myth: No narrative myth survives. The Mesha Stele gives Chemosh's theology: Omri king of Israel humbled Moab for many days 'because Chemosh was angry with his land'. Then Chemosh restored the land in Mesha's days. Chemosh told Mesha, 'Go, take Nebo from Israel', and Mesha killed its 7,000 inhabitants because he had devoted them (the same idea as the Hebrew herem, 'devotion to destruction') to Ashtar-Chemosh. He took the vessels of Yahweh from Nebo and dragged them before Chemosh. Chemosh 'drove out' the king of Israel before him.
biblicalRole:
Israel's songs taunt Moab as 'the people of Chemosh' whose sons and daughters became fugitives (Num 21:29; Jer 48:46). Jephthah tells the Ammonite king, 'Will you not possess what Chemosh your god gives you?', treating Chemosh as Ammon's god, either a slip, a sign that Ammon then ruled Moabite land, or a rhetorical move (Judg 11:24). Solomon built a high place for 'Chemosh the abomination of Moab' east of Jerusalem (1 Kgs 11:7); Josiah defiled it (2 Kgs 23:13). Jeremiah says Chemosh will go into exile with his priests and princes (Jer 48:7; Jer 48:13).

The most startling text is 2 Kgs 3. Mesha, king of Moab, a sheep-breeder who paid Israel huge tribute, rebelled after Ahab's death (2 Kgs 3:4-5). Israel, Judah and Edom invaded and besieged him at Kir-hareseth. In desperation Mesha offered his eldest son as a burnt offering on the wall, 'and there came great wrath against Israel', and they withdrew (2 Kgs 3:26-27). Whose wrath? Readings include: (1) Chemosh's wrath, the writer admitting the foreign god's power in his own land (a minority view); (2) Yahweh's wrath against Israel for some fault or for provoking the act; (3) human fury or horror, the Moabites' rage or Israel's own dismay, sapping their will; (4) the writer deliberately leaves it unexplained. The text does not say.

encounters.summary: Old war-songs and Jeremiah lament Moab as Chemosh's people, scattered and captive.

encounters.summary: Jephthah argues from each nation's god-given land: let Ammon keep what Chemosh gives, and Israel what Yahweh gives.

encounters.summary: Solomon builds a shrine to Chemosh 'on the mountain east of Jerusalem'.

encounters.summary: Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh as Israel was ashamed of Bethel.

archaeology.summary: A black basalt stele about 1.15 m tall with 34 lines in Moabite, c. 840 BC. The Anglican missionary F. A. Klein was shown it in 1868; while Prussian and French agents competed for it and Ottoman authorities pressed the local Bani Hamida, the locals heated it and poured cold water over it, shattering it (1869). Charles Clermont-Ganneau had already had a paper squeeze made, torn in haste while still wet. The stone was reconstructed from the squeeze and recovered fragments (about two-thirds of the original). It begins 'I am Mesha son of Chemosh-[yat], king of Moab, the Dibonite', names Omri and 'his son', records the taking of Nebo and the 'vessels of YHWH' dragged before Chemosh. It is the earliest certain mention of Yahweh outside the Bible. A reading of 'House of David' in line 31 (André Lemaire, 1994) is debated.
A small fragment naming '[Chemosh-yat], king of Moab', probably Mesha's father, confirming the Chemosh-based royal name.

The stele says Israel oppressed Moab under Omri and 'his son' (or descendant) for 40 years and that Mesha regained his land; Kings places Mesha's revolt after Ahab's death. Most scholars think both describe the same broad events from opposite sides, with chronological details hard to reconcile.

laterFate: Moab ceased to exist as a kingdom in the 6th century BC, and Chemosh vanished with it. Milton's *Paradise Lost* (Book 1) names 'Chemos, the obscene dread of Moab's sons', identifies him with Peor, and has him follow Moloch in the catalogue of fallen angels.

name: Rimmon
symbol: bull with a lightning bolt; possibly the pomegranate by the biblical pun

cultCenter.name: Temple of Hadad in Damascus (site of the later Temple of Jupiter and the Umayyad Mosque)

plain:
Rimmon was the storm god of Damascus, capital of Aram (Syria): the same Hadad that Canaanites called Baal, under his Akkadian title Ramman, 'the Thunderer'. Several Aramean kings carried his name: Ben-Hadad ('son of Hadad'), Hadadezer ('Hadad is help') and Tabrimmon ('Rimmon is good').

He appears in one of the Bible's most human scenes. Naaman, the Syrian general healed of skin disease by Elisha, promises to worship only Israel's God, but asks forgiveness in advance for when his king leans on his arm and he must bow with him in the house of Rimmon. Elisha simply says, 'Go in peace.'
myth: Hadad of Damascus was the Aramean storm god and divine king, in the same tradition as Baal of Ugarit and Adad of Assyria. Kings of Aram claimed he went before them in battle, as the Tel Dan inscription says of Hazael. The Akkadian epithet Ramman ('thunderer') became the Hebrew Rimmon, which also happens to be the ordinary word for 'pomegranate'.
biblicalRole:
Naaman asks for two mule-loads of Israelite earth so he can worship Yahweh in Damascus, a sign that he still thinks of gods as tied to their land. He also asks pardon for bowing with his king in the house of Rimmon, and Elisha replies, 'Go in peace' (2 Kgs 5:17-19). Christians have long debated whether this was a concession to weakness, tolerance of outward conformity, or simply a blessing on his departure without approving the request.

Ahaz copies the design of an altar he saw in Damascus and installs it in Yahweh's temple, sacrificing 'to the gods of Damascus that had struck him' (2 Kgs 16:10-16; 2 Chr 28:23). Zechariah speaks of a great mourning in Jerusalem 'like the mourning for Hadad-rimmon in the valley of Megiddo' (Zech 12:11). This may be ritual weeping for a dying storm god, or a place-name commemorating the mourning for King Josiah, killed at Megiddo; it is debated.
