renamed.explanation: Hebrew writers may have deliberately read the god's title as rimmon, 'pomegranate', making the mighty Thunderer a piece of fruit. Others think it is just the normal Hebrew form of the Aramaic name. The pun is possible but unproven.

laterFate: Hadad of Damascus became Jupiter Damascenus under Rome. Milton's *Paradise Lost* (Book 1) names 'Rimmon, whose delightful seat was fair Damascus', who won over Naaman's king and led Ahaz to copy his altar. The phrase 'bowing in the house of Rimmon' became an English idiom for compromising one's conscience to keep one's position.

name: Tammuz
domains: the dying of growth in summer
symbol: shepherd's crook; reed pipe; sheepfold

cultCenter.name: Uruk and Bad-tibira in southern Mesopotamia

family.relation: sister who shares his time in the underworld
family.name: Geshtinanna

plain:
Tammuz (Sumerian Dumuzi) was a shepherd god, husband of the love goddess Inanna (Ishtar). In Mesopotamian myth he was dragged down to the underworld, and each summer women mourned him with laments as the green pastures withered.

The Bible mentions him once. In a vision dated about 592 BC, Ezekiel is taken to the north gate of the Jerusalem temple and sees 'women sitting, weeping for Tammuz' (Ezek 8:14). The month of Tammuz still has his name in the Jewish calendar.
myth:
In the Sumerian 'Descent of Inanna', Inanna goes down to the underworld, dies there, and is revived on condition that she sends someone in her place. Returning, she finds her husband Dumuzi enthroned and unmoved by her absence, and hands him to the demons. Dumuzi's sister Geshtinanna mourns him and agrees to share his fate: each spends half the year below. (This ending was understood only in the 1960s; earlier scholars thought he simply stayed dead.) Many other Sumerian songs tell of the courtship of Inanna and Dumuzi and of laments for the slain shepherd.

Sir James Frazer's *The Golden Bough* (1890 onward) grouped Tammuz with Adonis, Osiris and Attis as 'dying and rising gods'. Later scholars, notably Jonathan Z. Smith, criticised that category as forced; others, such as Tryggve Mettinger, defend a modified version of it. It is a live debate.
biblicalRole:
Ezekiel's temple vision (Ezek 8) is a tour of four 'abominations', each worse than the last: an 'image of jealousy' at the north gate; seventy elders burning incense to drawings of creeping things and beasts; women weeping for Tammuz at the north gate of the temple; and twenty-five men with their backs to the temple, bowing east to the sun (Ezek 8:14-16). The point is that even in Jerusalem's last years before 586 BC, Judahites were mourning a Mesopotamian god at Yahweh's own house.

Some scholars suggest other veiled references: Isaiah's 'pleasant plants' or 'gardens of Adonis' planted for a foreign god (Isa 17:10-11), and Daniel's 'the one beloved by women' (Dan 11:37). These are speculative.

encounters.summary: At the north gate of the temple Ezekiel sees women mourning Tammuz, and is told he will see still greater abominations.

encounters.summary: The vision is dated to the sixth year of Jehoiachin's exile; it climaxes with sun worship in the inner court.

encounters.summary: Isaiah describes plants of pleasantness and a foreign slip that wither, which some connect with Adonis-gardens; speculative.

archaeology.year: tablets excavated mainly at Nippur, late 19th-20th century; reconstruction by Samuel Noah Kramer and others
archaeology.place: Nippur, Iraq (Old Babylonian copies, c. 1900-1600 BC)

archaeology.summary: A shorter Akkadian version ending with rites for Tammuz, showing the cult was alive in the 1st millennium BC, Ezekiel's era.
The fourth month (June-July) was named for Dumuzi in the Babylonian calendar; the Jews adopted these month names during and after the exile.

laterFate: Tammuz became identified with the Phoenician-Greek Adonis, whose name is Semitic adon, 'lord'. Jerome (Letter 58) complains that Bethlehem's birth-cave was overshadowed by a grove of Tammuz, that is, Adonis, in the 2nd-4th centuries. Maimonides (*Guide for the Perplexed* 3.29) retells a Sabian legend of Tammuz's death. Milton's *Paradise Lost* (Book 1) has 'Thammuz', whose yearly wound turned the river Adonis red and moved the daughters of Zion to the lament Ezekiel saw. The Jewish month and the Arabic Syrian month Tammuz still carry his name.

name: Queen of Heaven
otherNames: meleket ha-shamayim ('the work/host of heaven', Masoretic vowels)
possibly Astarte, Ishtar, Anat or Asherah
symbol: cakes (kawwanim) shaped or stamped with her image; the star

cultCenter.name: The streets of Jerusalem and the towns of Judah; later Judean refugee communities in Egypt

plain:
The 'Queen of Heaven' was a goddess worshipped by ordinary Judean families in Jeremiah's day, around 600 BC. Children gathered wood, fathers lit the fire, and women kneaded dough to bake cakes for her (Jer 7:18).

Jeremiah 44 gives one of the most revealing exchanges in the Bible. After Jerusalem fell, Judean refugees in Egypt told Jeremiah flatly that they would keep burning incense to the Queen of Heaven, because when they did, they had plenty of bread and were well, and since they stopped (under Josiah's reform) they had lacked everything. From their point of view, abandoning the goddess was what caused the disaster. Who exactly she was is not certain.
myth: Her worshippers did not leave us her stories under this title. If she was Ishtar, her myths include the descent to the underworld and her love for Tammuz; if Astarte, she was the Phoenician queen goddess of love and war; if Anat, Egyptian texts call Anat 'lady of heaven'. What the Bible does record is her worshippers' theology: a household goddess who repays faithful offerings with food, health and safety.
biblicalRole:
Jeremiah condemns the family cult of the Queen of Heaven in Jerusalem (Jer 7:16-20). Later, in Pathros in Upper Egypt, the women say their husbands knew and approved of their incense, drink offerings and cakes 'made in her image' (Jer 44:15-19). The men and women together vow to continue. Jeremiah replies that it was exactly this incense that God remembered and punished, and announces that Pharaoh Hophra will fall (Jer 44:20-30).

The identity of the Queen is debated. (1) Ishtar: 'Queen of Heaven' is a standard Akkadian title of Ishtar (sharrat shame), and the cakes recall Mesopotamian kamanu cakes offered to Ishtar; kawwanim is probably a loanword from that term. (2) Astarte: the western form of Ishtar, popular in the Levant and Egypt. (3) Anat. (4) Asherah. Many scholars (e.g. Susan Ackerman) argue she was a blend of Ishtar and Astarte. All agree she was a goddess of popular, family religion, and that women played the leading role in her cult.

archaeology.summary: Hundreds of household clay figurines of a woman supporting her breasts, c. 750-586 BC. Some scholars connect them with the Queen of Heaven or Asherah; others see generic fertility or protective charms.
Clay moulds of the 18th century BC from the palace kitchen include one shaped as a nude female figure, often cited as a parallel for cakes 'in her image'. The link is illustrative, not direct.

Aramaic family letters of c. 500 BC from Arameans in Egypt send greetings to a temple of the Queen of Heaven at Syene (Aswan), showing the title in use in the very region where Jeremiah's refugees settled.

renamed.biblical: meleket ha-shamayim (Masoretic vowels), probably 'the work' or 'host of heaven'
renamed.explanation: In Jeremiah the consonants mlkt are pointed by the Masoretes as meleket, not malkat, as if to avoid calling the goddess 'queen'. Ancient Greek translators and most modern versions read 'Queen of Heaven'. Whether the vowels were a deliberate avoidance or a genuine alternative reading is debated.

laterFate: In the 4th century AD Epiphanius of Salamis (*Panarion* 79) condemned the Collyridians, a group of women in Arabia who offered cakes to the Virgin Mary, explicitly comparing them to the cake-offerers of Jeremiah. The medieval Latin title of Mary, 'Regina Caeli' (Queen of Heaven), has prompted Protestant polemic linking Marian devotion with Jeremiah's goddess; Catholic and Orthodox writers reply that the title derives from Mary's role as mother of the Messiah-King and from Rev 12, not from Ishtar or Astarte, and that she is honoured, not worshipped as divine. Historians generally see no direct line of descent between the two.

name: Baal Hammon and Tanit
otherNames: Kronos and Hera / Saturn and Caelestis (Greek and Roman identifications)
symbol: the 'sign of Tanit': a triangle topped by a horizontal bar and a disc, like a stick figure with raised arms; crescent and disc

cultCenter.name: Tophet of Salammbo, Carthage (Tunisia)

family.name: Astarte (Tanit linked with her at Sarepta)

plain:
Baal Hammon and Tanit were the chief gods of Carthage, the Phoenician colony in North Africa founded from Tyre. They are not in the Bible. They are here because the Carthage 'tophet', a sacred area full of urns of burned babies and young animals dedicated to them, is the main archaeological evidence used to understand the biblical Topheth and the cult of Molech.

Whether the Carthaginians routinely sacrificed their children, as Greek and Roman writers said, or whether the tophet was a special cemetery for infants who died naturally, is one of the most heated debates in Mediterranean archaeology.
myth: Few Punic myths survive. Baal Hammon was the senior god, often shown as a bearded elder on a throne flanked by sphinxes; the Greeks equated him with Kronos and the Romans with Saturn. The meaning of 'Hammon' is debated: 'lord of the incense altar' (compare the Hebrew hammanim, incense altars, in Lev 26:30 and Isa 17:8), or 'lord of Mount Amanus' in Syria. Tanit, called 'face of Baal', rose to prominence in Carthage from the 5th century BC and was later worshipped as Juno Caelestis. Inscriptions on the tophet stelae follow a set formula: 'To the Lady Tanit, face of Baal, and to the Lord Baal Hammon, what X son of Y vowed, because he heard his voice.'
biblicalRole: Neither god is named in the Bible. The connection is through practice. The Bible describes a 'Topheth' in the Hinnom valley where children were burned (Jer 7:31; 2 Kgs 23:10), calls the practice making children 'pass through the fire' (Deut 18:10; 2 Kgs 16:3), and says Phoenician-influenced kings brought foreign customs into Israel (1 Kgs 16:31). Scholars borrowed the biblical word 'tophet' for the Punic sanctuaries. Carthage's Punic inscriptions also use mlk as a sacrifice term, which led Otto Eissfeldt to his theory about Molech. The Bible's own word hammanim, incense altars that God threatens to destroy, may share a root with Baal Hammon's name (Lev 26:30; 2 Chr 34:4), though this is uncertain.

archaeology.year: discovered 1921 (F. Icard and P. Gielly); excavated 1920s-1940s and 1976-1979 (Lawrence Stager)
archaeology.summary: A sacred precinct used from about the 8th century BC until Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BC, with layer upon layer of urns holding the burned bones of infants, young children and young animals (lambs, kids), under stone markers and inscribed stelae to Tanit and Baal Hammon. Stager estimated about 20,000 urns were deposited between c. 400 and 200 BC alone. Similar tophets exist in Sicily (Motya), Sardinia (Tharros, Sulcis) and Malta.

Jeffrey Schwartz and colleagues (*PLoS ONE*, 2010) found that many of the infants were prenatal or perinatal and argued the tophet was a cemetery for babies who died naturally. Patricia Smith, Lawrence Stager and colleagues (*Antiquity*, 2011 and 2013), correcting for shrinkage of burned bone, found that the ages cluster at one to two months after birth, which fits a pattern of sacrifice rather than natural mortality. Other specialists (e.g. Paolo Xella and colleagues, *Antiquity* 2013) argue the inscriptions, which speak of vows and offerings, plus the classical sources, point to sacrifice. The question is still debated, though many specialists now accept that at least some infants were sacrificed.

archaeology.year: 1st century BC to 2nd century AD writings
archaeology.summary: Diodorus Siculus (*Library* 20.14) says that in 310 BC, besieged by Agathocles, Carthage sacrificed some 200-500 children of noble families to Kronos, whose bronze statue had outstretched hands from which the child rolled into a pit of fire. Plutarch (*On Superstition* 13) describes drums and flutes drowning the cries. Tertullian (*Apology* 9) says children were sacrificed to Saturn in Africa into Roman times. These writers were Carthage's enemies or outsiders, so their reliability is part of the debate.
A 7th-century BC ivory plaque dedicated to 'Tanit-Ashtart', showing Tanit was known in the Phoenician homeland and linked with Astarte.

laterFate: After Rome destroyed Carthage, Baal Hammon lived on as Saturn, whose cult was hugely popular in Roman North Africa, and Tanit as Juno Caelestis. Augustine (*City of God* 2.4) recalls the lewd festivals of the 'Virgin Caelestis' he watched as a young man in Carthage. Gustave Flaubert's novel *Salammbo* (1862) made the image of Carthaginian child sacrifice to Moloch famous in European imagination.

name: Sun, Moon and the Host of Heaven
otherNames: horses and chariots of the sun
domains: sun, moon and stars as divine powers
justice and seeing all things (the sun)
symbol: winged sun disc; horses and chariots of the sun; crescent moon; stars

cultCenter.name: The Jerusalem temple courts and rooftops of Jerusalem

family.relation: Venus, the morning and evening star
family.name: Ishtar

plain:
Ancient peoples around Israel worshipped the sun, the moon and the stars as gods: Shamash the sun god of justice in Mesopotamia, Sin the moon god of Harran and Ur, and the planets and constellations as divine beings who shaped fate. The Bible calls them 'the host of heaven'.

In Judah's last century this worship came right into the temple. Manasseh built altars for the host of heaven in its courts; there were horses dedicated to the sun at the temple entrance and 'chariots of the sun'; people burned incense on their rooftops to the stars. Josiah swept it all away, and Ezekiel still saw twenty-five men in the inner court bowing east to the sun with their backs to God's house.
myth: In Mesopotamia Shamash crossed the sky each day in his chariot and passed through the underworld at night, seeing everything; so he was the god of justice and oaths (he hands Hammurabi his laws on the famous stele). Sin the moon god kept time and gave omens. Babylonian astrology read the will of the gods in the stars. In Ugarit the sun was a goddess, Shapash, 'torch of the gods', who helps find the dead Baal. Judah stood between these worlds, and Assyrian domination in the 8th-7th centuries BC brought more astral religion with it, though how much was imposed and how much was local is debated.
biblicalRole:
Genesis deliberately calls the sun and moon just 'the greater light' and 'the lesser light', lamps God hung in the sky, perhaps to avoid names that were also gods' names (Gen 1:16; a common but debated reading). Deuteronomy warns Israel not to bow down to the sun, moon and stars, which God 'allotted to all the peoples' (Deut 4:19; Deut 17:3). Job protests that he never kissed his hand to the shining sun or moon (Job 31:26-28).

The northern kingdom worshipped the host of heaven (2 Kgs 17:16). Manasseh built altars for all the host of heaven in both temple courts (2 Kgs 21:3; 2 Kgs 21:5). Josiah removed the priests who burned incense 'to Baal, to the sun and the moon and the constellations and all the host of the heavens', took away the horses the kings had dedicated to the sun at the temple entrance, burned the chariots of the sun, and pulled down the rooftop altars of Ahaz (2 Kgs 23:4-5; 2 Kgs 23:11-12). Jeremiah and Zephaniah condemn rooftop offerings to the host of heaven (Jer 19:13; Zeph 1:5). Ezekiel sees about twenty-five men in the inner court facing east and bowing to the sun (Ezek 8:16).

At the same time the Bible uses solar language for God: 'the LORD God is a sun and shield' (Ps 84:11); 'the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings' (Mal 4:2). Some scholars (notably J. Glen Taylor, *Yahweh and the Sun*, 1993) argue that some Judahites actually worshipped Yahweh in solar form, so the 'horses of the sun' were Yahweh's; others think they were for a separate sun god introduced under Assyrian influence. It is debated.

Some (Taylor, Hestrin) read the top tier as Yahweh symbolised by a solar animal and alternating tiers as Yahweh and Asherah; others see generic Canaanite imagery.

archaeology.summary: Iron Age clay horse figurines, some with a disc on the forehead, have been linked to the 'horses of the sun' of 2 Kgs 23:11. Whether the disc is a sun or simply a forelock or ornament is debated.

archaeology.find: Hezekiah's royal seal impression and LMLK jar handles
archaeology.year: LMLK handles since the 19th century; Hezekiah bulla found 2009, published 2015 (Eilat Mazar)
archaeology.summary: A clay bulla reading 'belonging to Hezekiah son of Ahaz, king of Judah' carries a two-winged sun disc; many royal LMLK storage-jar handles bear a winged sun or four-winged scarab. These show solar symbols as royal emblems of Judah; whether they imply sun worship or simply borrowed Egyptian royal iconography is debated.

archaeology.find: Shamash on the Code of Hammurabi stele
archaeology.summary: The sun god Shamash, with rays rising from his shoulders, hands King Hammurabi (18th century BC) the symbols of authority: the classic image of the sun as god of justice.

laterFate: After the exile, Jewish practice made a point of turning away from sun worship: the Mishnah (*Sukkah* 5:4) records that during the Feast of Tabernacles priests turned toward the temple and declared that their fathers had turned their backs on the temple and bowed east to the sun, 'but as for us, our eyes are to the LORD'. The Roman cult of Sol Invictus later became a major rival to early Christianity; early Christians themselves prayed facing east toward the rising sun as a symbol of Christ's return, while insisting they did not worship the sun (Tertullian answers this charge in *Apology* 16). Astrology, the heir of star worship, has never fully gone away.
